prize_parts.citation: for showing how technology and trade shocks reshape labour demand, job polarisation and the fortunes of local labour markets

statement.case_for: I now prefer B009 to my opening first choice, B016. The Autor-Dorn-Hanson work combines a clear conceptual idea (tasks, polarisation) with transparent, replicable research designs: import-competition exposure, local labour-market outcomes, and administrative or census-style data that others can re-run. It has produced a large body of follow-up studies and robustness checks, and its core finding of persistent local adjustment costs has held up. It also changed policy debate on trade and automation. Autor-Dorn (2013) is itself a task-based polarisation paper, so Dorn credibly covers both the technology and the trade strands. A trio of Autor, Dorn and Hanson therefore gives a coherent citation and a cleaner credit boundary than adding the longer skill-premium line.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the shift-share exposure designs behind the China-shock estimates are the subject of live inference and identification debate, and the persistence and external validity of the effects are still being refined. The topic also overlaps in theme with the 2023 and 2024 prizes on labour-market outcomes and on technology and institutions. Leaving out Katz, whose skill-premium and education-technology work is foundational, is a real attribution cost.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B009 first and proposes Autor, Hanson and Dorn. He ties the China-shock work to those three, treats Katz as a parallel contributor on wage inequality, and worries that the credit boundary is contestable.
responses.response: I now agree with his trio over my opening Autor-Hanson-Katz. Katz's most prominent work on education and technology is closely tied to Goldin's research, which the committee recognised in 2023. That makes the marginal credit harder to defend, and it shifts the prize toward a stranger-to-stranger comparison with a prior award. The Autor-Dorn-Hanson set also rests on designs that outside researchers can and have re-run. I qualify his point in one respect: a citation centred only on the trade shock would understate the task and polarisation strand, so I would keep the citation broad. Dorn's co-authored polarisation work supports that.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B009 first but flags debate over the persistence and external validity of the shift-share trade-shock estimates. He also asks how much the 2024 prize and Goldin's 2023 prize already cover this ground.
responses.response: I share the shift-share concern, and it is the main reason I do not treat the case as settled. In my view it is a reason to look at the replication record rather than to discount the work. The core findings on adjustment costs have survived many re-analyses, and the debate has mostly refined magnitudes. On overlap, Acemoglu's recognised work is on directed technology and growth, while this body of work is empirical evidence on displacement and local adjustment. I think the citation can be written to keep the two distinct, but I accept that this is a judgement the committee needs to make explicitly.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B014 first. He gives the heterogeneous-firm framework a very strong case, noting its influence across macro, growth and IO. He ranks B016 fifth and notes that confirmation of taxable-income elasticities is mixed and that Chetty's and Saez's credit is split across other candidacies.
responses.response: His assessment of B016 is fair, and it is the main reason I moved it from my first choice to an alternative. Elasticity estimates vary with setting and specification, and credit overlaps across B036 and B050. On B014, I agree it is mature and influential. I ranked it sixth because Krugman's 2008 prize covers part of the antecedent trade theory, because Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are uncredited, and because the size of welfare gains from selection is contested. Those points matter to me more than they seem to for him, and I would like to hear how he weighs them against the framework's reach.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B050 first, arguing that population-scale administrative data plus a framework for causal place effects is a major contribution. She also notes the three-person cap forces choices among Chetty, Hendren and Friedman.
responses.response: I value the data-construction and transparency side of this work, and I see why it is attractive. My hesitation is maturity and attribution. The main results are about a decade old, credit is spread over a large team, and the causal interpretation of neighbourhood effects is still being tested. I would revisit it in a later year, but I do not think it is ready to be the preferred prize now.

uncertainties: Whether Katz or Dorn belongs in the final trio, and whether the committee would rather cite the trade-shock evidence and the task framework as one achievement or two.
How far the shift-share inference debate and the persistence of local effects should temper the claims in a citation.
How much of the technology and inequality ground is already covered by the 2023 and 2024 prizes.
Whether the three-person cap can be reconciled with the credit owed to Levy and Murnane on the task framework, who are not on the list.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the preferred laureates (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) or for the alternatives I name. The profile lists co-authors in behavioural and metascience research, and none of them is a candidate on my preferred or alternative parts.
